Name: compositional_feature_steering
Title: Do Interpretable Features Compose? A Causal Test of Multi-Constraint Steering in Biomolecular Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: If sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features of protein language models are genuinely disentangled causal handles, then simultaneously steering along several feature directions under a fixed steering budget should compose approximately additively: the joint effect superposes the solo effects, satisfying multiple design constraints at once with low interference and preserved validity, whereas norm-matched raw-activation steering shows destructive interference. We further hypothesize a null: a feature's interpretability score (concept correlation) does NOT predict its compositional steerability, and that low-alpha causal-effect magnitude and decoder-direction geometry do. Ranked by centrality, the contributions are: (1) the empirical compositionality test, (2) a predictive rule for which features compose, and (3) a geometric orthogonalization fix.
Related Work: A rapidly growing body of work applies sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to protein language models for single-property steering: InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE (RFdiffusion), MotifAE, ProtoMech (cross-layer transcoders), and antibody/RNA SAEs. Critically, every one of these steers toward ONE target property (e.g., a zinc-finger motif, thermostability) and evaluates only whether that single property appears; none report joint success under two or more simultaneous constraints, none quantify cross-feature interference, and none provide a predictor of which features can be combined. The antibody SAE paper (2025) reports the crucial anomaly that high feature-concept correlation does NOT guarantee causal steerability, but does not explain what does, nor study multi-property control. Our proposal is the first to systematically test COMPOSITIONALITY: whether independently identified feature directions can be combined to satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously, and to turn that incidental anomaly into a testable, generalizable predictor. This matters because real design workflows (enzyme engineering, antibody optimization, de novo scaffolds) routinely require several constraints at once (fold AND stability AND a functional motif AND localization), so single-property steerability does not establish practical controllability.
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose protein language model (pLM) activations into human-interpretable features, and recent work shows individual features can steer generation toward single target properties. Real biomolecular design, however, requires satisfying multiple constraints at once (e.g., a specific fold AND high thermostability AND a binding motif AND a localization signal). We ask a simple, falsifiable question: do interpretable features COMPOSE? If features are truly disentangled causal handles, steering along several feature directions simultaneously under a fixed budget should approximately superpose their individual effects, hitting multiple targets with little interference and preserved sequence validity. We test this on ESM-2 with SAEs trained on its residual stream, defining an Interference Score (degradation of each property when co-steered versus solo) and a Validity Budget (steering strength before sequences become non-viable, measured by pseudo-perplexity, ESMFold pLDDT, and property predictors). Across pre-registered pairs and triples of properties (secondary-structure content, thermostability proxy, hydrophobicity/GRAVY, catalytic-site motifs), we compare SAE-feature steering against norm-matched raw-activation, random, PCA, and top-activation baselines, and against orthogonalized-feature steering. We then test whether interpretability score predicts compositional steerability, and whether low-alpha causal-effect magnitude and decoder geometry predict it instead. We expect SAE features to compose more gracefully than raw steering but to exhibit systematic interference clusters, and that steerability is predicted by causal-effect magnitude rather than concept correlation. Results yield a practical recipe for multi-constraint design, a rule for selecting compositionally steerable features, and a mechanistic account of when interpretable features act as independent design levers.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP (used by every experiment below). Model: frozen ESM-2 650M (33 layers, hidden width 1280) as primary and frozen ESM-2 150M (30 layers, width 640) as a size-robustness check; both are the public facebook/esm masked protein LMs, weights never updated. Interpretability handles: a TopK sparse autoencoder (SAE; k=32 active latents, dictionary 16,384) trained on residual-stream activations at one layer selected by the intrinsic-dimension elbow (expected near the middle block); a Matryoshka SAE is trained as an architecture-robustness variant. SAE training data: 20M residual-stream token-activations sampled from a 500k-sequence subset of UniRef50 (~60M sequences available; 500k chosen to keep one training run under a day on a single A100); Adam, lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, one training pass, 3 SAE seeds. "Steering" = adding alpha times a unit direction (the SAE decoder column, or a baseline direction) to the chosen layer at all positions during masked-infill generation. Property evaluators (all automated, no wet lab): alpha-helix % and beta-sheet % from DSSP run on ESMFold structures; GRAVY hydrophobicity and molecular weight from Biopython; a thermostability proxy from a ridge head fit on the Meltome Atlas (~48k proteins, held-out R^2 reported); two motifs (C2H2 zinc-finger, Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad) via PROSITE regex/HMMER. FEATURE-SELECTION PROTOCOL (pre-registered to prevent a hand-picked easy-pair benchmark): for each property, features above a fixed concept-correlation floor on 5k held-out UniRef sequences are frozen into a bank BEFORE any co-steering is run; the single best per property gives a ~7-feature bank, expanded to ~30-40 for the regression analyses. All property pairs/triples are enumerated exhaustively (no hand-picking). Generation uses 5 sampling seeds; 200 sequences per condition. All correlations report 95% bootstrap CIs and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the many pairs/triples.

Experiment 1 (H1 - additive composition of SAE features): Tests whether co-steering several SAE feature directions at once satisfies several constraints simultaneously with minimal interference and preserved validity. Decisive metric: joint success rate = fraction of generated sequences meeting ALL targeted property thresholds at once. Secondary: per-property Interference Score I = (solo gain - co-steered gain)/solo gain. Convincing result: joint success >= 0.6x the product of the features' solo success rates AND mean I <= 0.2 while the fraction of foldable sequences (ESMFold pLDDT >= 70) falls by < 10 points versus solo steering. Decision band (indeterminate): mean I in [0.2, 0.4] OR joint success in [0.4, 0.6]x the product -> report "partial composition," which neither confirms additive composition nor the destructive alternative, and defer the verdict to the geometric analysis in Experiment 4. Negative result (mean I > 0.4 or joint success < 0.4x product) means SAE features do NOT compose additively, refuting H1. Data/systems: all 21 property PAIRS and 10 TRIPLES from the ~7-feature bank, each co-steered at its solo-calibrated alpha (calibrated by a prior per-feature strength sweep recording property gain vs validity). A realistic-design subset couples fold + thermostability + catalytic-triad motif to mirror an enzyme-engineering objective and is reported separately. Robustness: repeat a reduced 3-property protocol on the RiNALMo RNA LM (~650M, frozen) with 2 RNA properties (GC content, a stem-loop motif) to check the compositionality principle transfers across biomolecule type.

Experiment 2 (H2 - raw-activation steering shows destructive interference): Tests the claimed contrast that raw-activation steering interferes where SAE steering does not. Decisive metric: paired difference in mean Interference Score, (raw minus SAE), across the same 21 pairs and 10 triples. Convincing result: norm-matched raw difference-of-means steering (directions matched to each SAE feature's solo property gain and in norm) shows mean I higher by >= 0.15 with a 95% bootstrap CI excluding 0, and lower joint success. Decision band: difference in [0.0, 0.15] -> the two are indistinguishable on interference; report that SAE features offer no compositional advantage over raw steering (a partial refutation of the framing). Negative result (raw I <= SAE I) refutes H2. Systems compared (all norm-matched): (a) additive SAE-feature steering, (b) raw difference-of-means directions, (c) random directions, (d) PCA-of-activations directions, (e) top-activation-token directions, (f) Gram-Schmidt-orthogonalized SAE directions (feeds Experiment 4c).

Experiment 3 (H3 - interpretability score does not predict compositional steerability): Tests whether a feature's concept-correlation predicts how well it composes. Decisive metric: Spearman rho(concept-correlation, compositional steerability), where steerability = 1 - mean I over that feature's pairings. Convincing result for H3 (a null): |rho| <= 0.2 with 95% bootstrap CI contained in [-0.4, 0.4]. Decision band: |rho| in [0.2, 0.4] -> weak, ambiguous predictive value; report as "not clearly predictive." Negative result (rho >= 0.4) means interpretability DOES predict compositional steerability, refuting H3. Data: the ~7-feature bank is small, so we use the pre-registered expanded bank of ~30-40 property-linked features to power this regression, reported with n, CIs, and BH correction.

Experiment 4 (H4 - identifying what does predict it, and a geometric fix): Tests the positive companion to H3: that causal-effect magnitude and decoder geometry predict compositional steerability and that pre-orthogonalization repairs interference. (a) Predictor test - decisive metric Spearman rho(causal-effect magnitude, steerability), where causal magnitude = property change per unit alpha at low alpha; convincing if rho >= 0.5 AND exceeds the concept-correlation rho of Experiment 3 by >= 0.2. (b) Interference geometry - decisive metric rho(|decoder-direction cosine|, pairwise Interference Score) across all feature pairs; convincing if rho >= 0.5. (c) Fix - Gram-Schmidt pre-orthogonalize colliding feature pairs and re-run co-steering; convincing if mean I drops by >= 0.15 absolute with joint success rising and validity retained, while we report the interpretability cost (change in the orthogonalized direction's concept-correlation). Decision band: causal rho in [0.3, 0.5], or geometry rho in [0.3, 0.5], or interference reduction in [0.05, 0.15] -> suggestive but not decisive; report the predictor as a candidate needing more features. Negative result (no predictor beats chance and orthogonalization does not reduce interference) means we fail to identify what governs compositional steerability, so the hypothesis's "we identify what property does" clause is unsupported. Practical payoff: the winning predictor becomes a cheap pre-screen for feature selection, changing steering strategy from "pick the most interpretable feature" to "pick the strongest causal, geometrically non-colliding feature."
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Property evaluators (structure/thermostability predictors) are imperfect proxies for wet-lab truth; conclusions are about in-silico controllability, not experimentally validated function. 2) Compositionality may be trivially poor if all chosen features live in a low-dimensional subspace; we mitigate by selecting features spanning diverse concept types and reporting the full interference matrix. 3) SAE quality and layer choice could confound results; we control by comparing multiple SAE architectures (TopK, Matryoshka) and model sizes, and by steering-magnitude sweeps. 4) The predictive-regression analysis could be underpowered if the feature bank is small; we mitigate by the pre-registered expanded bank of tens of features and report n, CIs, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the many pairs/triples. 5) The feature bank and all pairs/triples are frozen before co-steering to prevent cherry-picking of easy pairs. 6) Orthogonalization may reduce interpretability of steered directions, a tradeoff we quantify rather than assume away. 7) The predictor claim is presented as an empirical, falsifiable rule, not a proven mechanistic theory.

Name: feature_steering_rare_region_design
Title: Steering Off the Mode: Can Interpretable Features Guide Generative Protein Models Into Rare-but-Valid Design Space?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable SAE features act as directional handles that let protein language models reach LOW-likelihood-but-still-valid regions of sequence space (rare folds/motifs/property combinations) that likelihood-guided sampling systematically undersamples, and they do so more efficiently and with higher validity than raw activation steering or temperature/top-p sampling. 'Off-mode' here is a directed, controllable displacement toward a chosen property band while staying on the valid-sequence manifold, distinct from undirected diversity sampling that merely raises entropy. We further hypothesize that a feature's causal steering strength, not its concept-correlation, predicts how far off-mode it can push generation while retaining validity. The core novelty is a new objective: distributional escape with validity preservation, measured by a Reach-Validity Frontier.
Related Work: Existing SAE-and-steering work for protein LMs (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'Steering Protein Language Models'/ASPO 2025; the antibody SAE paper 2025; ProtoMech cross-layer transcoders 2026; Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B 2025) all evaluate whether steering INCREASES a single target property near the model's high-likelihood modes; none quantify how far generation can be pushed away from the mode while remaining valid. A recent review (Guiding Generative Models for Protein Design, 2025) explicitly flags that generative models undersample low-probability regions that often encode valuable properties, but proposes no interpretability-based remedy. SAE-Targeted Steering (Chalnev et al. 2024) improves side-effect control in text LMs but does not study distributional escape or rare-region reachability. Our proposal is the first to reframe interpretable-feature steering as a controlled DISTRIBUTION-ESCAPE tool for scientific design: quantifying how far off-mode features can drive valid generation, comparing against non-interpretable exploration baselines under matched budgets, and testing what feature property predicts safe off-mode reach. Concretely it targets lead diversification, scaffold hopping, and hitting rare function combinations, and would be adopted first by protein-engineering, generative-design, and interpretability communities; the Reach-Validity Frontier is proposed as a reusable benchmark for exploration methods. This turns interpretability from a descriptive add-on into a diversity-and-novelty engine.
Abstract: Generative protein models sample most heavily from the high-likelihood modes of their training distribution, systematically neglecting rare regions of sequence space that may encode novel, valuable designs. Prior interpretability work shows that sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features of protein language models can steer generation toward single target properties, but always tests gains near the model's comfortable modes. We ask a different question: can interpretable features be used as controllable handles to push generation OFF the mode, into low-likelihood but still-valid sequence space, more efficiently and safely than non-interpretable exploration methods? Unlike undirected diversity sampling, this is a directed displacement toward a target property band that stays on the valid manifold. We train SAEs on ESM-2 residual streams and, for each of a bank of property-linked features, sweep steering strength while tracking distributional escape (drop in sequence likelihood / distance from the natural-sequence manifold) and validity (ESMFold pLDDT, pseudo-perplexity, property-predictor agreement, novelty checks) jointly. We define a Reach-Validity Frontier and compare feature steering against raw difference-of-means steering, high-temperature/top-p sampling, and random-direction perturbation under matched sample and likelihood-drop budgets. We hypothesize that (i) interpretable features achieve a strictly better Reach-Validity frontier than non-directional exploration, (ii) they unlock rare property COMBINATIONS absent from natural training data while remaining foldable, and (iii) a feature's measured causal effect magnitude, not its concept-correlation, predicts how far off-mode it can safely reach. Results would establish interpretable features as an efficient, controllable engine for exploring novel scientific design space, provide a reusable exploration benchmark, and give a mechanistic account of which features are trustworthy exploration directions.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: frozen ESM-2 150M (30 layers, width 640) and ESM-2 650M (33 layers, width 1280), public facebook/esm masked protein LMs, weights frozen. Handles: TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on residual-stream activations at the intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer, plus a Matryoshka SAE for robustness; trained on 20M activation-tokens from a 500k-sequence UniRef50 subset (~60M available; 500k for one-day single-A100 training), Adam lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, 3 SAE seeds. Feature bank: ~30-50 features mapped to measurable properties - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY and molecular weight (Biopython), a thermostability proxy (ridge head on Meltome Atlas ~48k proteins), and 2 motifs (C2H2 zinc-finger, catalytic triad; PROSITE/HMMER). Validity is required to pass FOUR orthogonal checks: ESMFold pLDDT >= 70 (structure confidence), pseudo-perplexity below the natural-set 95th percentile (sequence plausibility), property-predictor agreement, and a novelty screen (not a trivial repeat/low-complexity artifact). Generation: 5 seeds, 200 sequences per condition. Off-mode reach for a sequence = its negative log-likelihood under ESM-2 minus the unsteered-baseline mean, combined with embedding kNN distance to its nearest neighbor in a held-out 100k-sequence UniRef sample. 'Causal steering strength' of a feature = property change per unit steering coefficient measured near alpha=0 (finite-difference slope), reported for robustness across 3 candidate layers, both model sizes, and both SAE architectures.

Experiment 1 (H1 - interpretable features dominate the reach-validity frontier): Tests whether SAE-feature steering reaches lower-likelihood but still-valid sequence space than likelihood-based sampling, at higher reach for equal validity than raw-activation steering and than temperature/top-p sampling. Decisive metric: reach-validity frontier area (off-mode reach on one axis, fraction of generations still valid on the other), per method. Convincing result: SAE-feature frontier area exceeds every baseline by >= 15% relative, paired across features and seeds (95% CI excludes 0), and SAE dominates (higher reach at equal validity) for >= 70% of features. Decision band: relative advantage in [5%, 15%] -> marginal; report SAE as competitive but not clearly dominant. Negative result (< 5% or a baseline on top) refutes H1. Systems (matched budgets: equal sample count and, where applicable, matched mean likelihood drop): (i) SAE-feature steering, (ii) raw difference-of-means steering, (iii) high-temperature sampling, (iv) top-p sampling, (v) random residual perturbation matched in norm; temperature and top-p are swept over >= 8 settings each to give the strongest fair baseline. Ablations: feature-selection criterion (concept-correlation floor vs causal-effect ranking), steering-vector normalization (unit vs raw decoder), and the likelihood-drop vs validity tradeoff curve.

Experiment 2 (H2 - unlocking rare property combinations): Tests whether features generate valid foldable sequences hitting property combinations that are anti-correlated or absent in nature - the lead-diversification/scaffold-hopping use case. Decisive metric: valid rare-target success rate = fraction of generations that pass all validity checks and simultaneously hit both targeted property bands. Convincing result: SAE steering success >= 2x the best baseline's success AND >= 0.10 in absolute terms (so the win is not 0.01 vs 0.005). Decision band: SAE success between 1.2x and 2x the best baseline -> a real but modest unlock; report as partial support. Negative result (SAE <= 1.2x baseline) refutes H2. Data/targets: 5 target combinations chosen as anti-correlated or unseen in a 100k UniRef sample (e.g., high beta-sheet + high hydrophilicity; two motifs that rarely co-occur), each with 200 generations x 5 seeds; novelty of successes reported as max identity to any natural sequence and embedding distance.

Experiment 3 (H3 - causal steering strength, not concept-correlation, predicts safe off-mode reach): Tests which feature property predicts how far off-mode a feature can push while staying valid. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between a candidate predictor and each feature's frontier area (safe off-mode reach) from Experiment 1. Convincing result: causal-effect magnitude attains rho >= 0.5 and exceeds concept-correlation's rho by >= 0.2, while concept-correlation's rho lies within [-0.2, 0.2]. Decision band: causal rho in [0.3, 0.5], or its margin over concept-correlation in [0.1, 0.2] -> suggestive only. Negative result (concept-correlation predicts as well as or better than causal magnitude) refutes H3. Predictors also computed: decoder-direction norm/orthogonality to the natural-sequence manifold, and monosemanticity; regression uses the full ~30-50 feature bank with bootstrap CIs. Generalization: a reduced protocol on the p-IgGen antibody LM (~17M) and a GPT-style SMILES molecular LM tests whether frontier dominance transfers across object types.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico validity (ESMFold pLDDT, predictors) is a proxy for wet-lab function; claims are scoped to controllable exploration of model-defined valid space, not experimental viability, and no wet-lab validation is performed. 2) 'Off-mode' reach measured by model likelihood may conflate genuinely novel-but-valid sequences with degenerate artifacts; we mitigate via four independent validity signals and novelty checks against natural databases. 3) High-temperature/top-p baselines may be tuned suboptimally; we sweep them thoroughly and match sample and likelihood-drop budgets to give the strongest fair comparison. 4) The predictor-regression may be underpowered with a modest feature bank; mitigated by using tens of features across property types, multiple seeds, and bootstrap CIs. 5) Frontier dominance could be model/SAE-specific; mitigated by testing two model sizes, two SAE architectures, three layers, and a cross-domain object type.

Name: steerability_predictor
Title: Decodable but Inert: A Predictive Theory of Which Interpretable Directions Actually Steer Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: Across biomolecular generative models, whether an interpretable/linearly-decodable direction is causally steerable is NOT random noise but is predicted by cheap, intervention-free geometric quantities computed at the intervention site. Falsifiable core claim: the alignment between the direction and the model's local property-output Jacobian at the intervention layer (how much the downstream computation actually reads that direction) forecasts steering efficacy with higher rank correlation than concept-correlation, probe accuracy, decoder norm, or raw-gradient cosine, across the specified models and sites. This enables a pre-flight test that selects effective steering directions before any generation. If cross-domain generality is weak, we narrow the claim to the smallest family in which it holds.
Related Work: Multiple recent papers independently report the same anomaly: high feature-concept correlation or linear decodability does not guarantee causal steering. The antibody SAE paper (2025) finds TopK SAE features are interpretable but not steerable. The Boltz-1 paper (Jedryszek et al. 2026) finds a beta-strand direction with F1=0.82 that produces zero causal effect. FEGA (Hoang et al. 2026) shows most SAE features lack a stable steering direction and distinguishes value-like vs pointer-like features by their logit-effect geometry. Each treats this as an obstacle or a descriptive taxonomy, and none provides a cheap PREDICTIVE test of steerability nor validates such a predictor as a screening tool across scientific object types. Prior text-LM work on predicting steering utility or side-effects (e.g., SAE-Targeted Steering) targets language attributes and does not use an intervention-free Jacobian-alignment geometry at the biomolecular intervention site. Prior steering work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE, ProtoMech, Matryoshka-SAE) demonstrates steering succeeds for SOME directions but selects them by trial-and-error generation. The concrete problem we target is the expensive generation-based screening of candidate steering directions in scientific design loops. Our proposal turns the shared anomaly into a positive, testable theory and a pre-flight filter, distinct from all prior descriptive or single-direction steering work.
Abstract: A striking anomaly recurs across mechanistic-interpretability studies of scientific generative models: directions that are highly interpretable and linearly decodable frequently produce no causal effect when used to steer generation. Antibody, protein, and structure-prediction studies each independently report this decodable-but-inert phenomenon, yet none explains what distinguishes steerable from inert directions or offers a way to predict steerability before running expensive generation experiments - the bottleneck in direction-based scientific design loops. We propose a predictive theory. Our central hypothesis is that steerability is governed by how strongly the model's downstream computation actually reads a direction at the intervention site, captured by the alignment between the direction and the local property-output Jacobian (the sensitivity of generated properties to activation perturbations). We define a small set of cheap, intervention-free candidate predictors - Jacobian alignment, decoder-direction norm relative to the residual stream, effective read-out via attention/MLP weight projections, raw-gradient cosine, and value-like vs pointer-like effect geometry - and benchmark them against ground-truth steering efficacy measured by property change per unit steer. We evaluate across ESM-2 protein LMs, an antibody LM (p-IgGen), and a SMILES molecular LM, using SAE features and difference-of-means directions, with a pre-registered held-out split so the predictor is never fit per domain. We test whether Jacobian alignment predicts steerability with high rank correlation while concept-correlation and probe accuracy do not, and validate a resulting 'steerability score' as a pre-flight filter that selects effective directions without generation, quantifying generation runs saved. Results would convert a widespread nuisance into an actionable, empirically validated screening principle for controllable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (three families, all frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (masked protein LM), p-IgGen antibody LM (~17M), and a GPT-style SMILES molecular LM (~10M, trained on a ~1.9M-molecule ChEMBL subset or a public checkpoint). Directions bank per model: 40-80 strongly decodable directions - TopK SAE features (and Ordered/Matryoshka where available) with high concept-correlation, plus difference-of-means directions for each measurable property. Properties with cheap evaluators: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex); antibodies - CDR length, net charge, a developability proxy; molecules - logP, QED, ring count, functional-group presence (RDKit SMARTS). GEOMETRY DEFINITION: at a fixed intervention layer L (residual stream), the property-Jacobian J is the gradient of a differentiable property surrogate with respect to the layer-L activation, averaged over a held-out set; Jacobian alignment of a unit direction d is ||proj_d J|| / ||J|| (the fraction of local property sensitivity captured by d), reported at L and swept over 3 candidate layers. Ground-truth steerability of a direction = slope of target-property change per unit steer at low strength, plus the max reliable property gain before validity collapses (validity: pseudo-perplexity/ESMFold pLDDT for proteins, RDKit-validity for molecules); measured over a strength sweep, 5 generation seeds. For non-differentiable evaluators (HMMER, folding) a lightweight differentiable surrogate supplies the Jacobian; surrogate held-out fidelity (R^2/AUROC) is reported. PRE-REGISTRATION: directions and models are split into a fit set (for choosing predictor normalization) and a held-out test set (for all reported rho and precision), fixed before ground-truth steering is measured.

Experiment 1 (H1+H2 - a cheap geometric quantity predicts steerability better than concept-correlation): Tests that causal steerability is non-randomly predicted by intervention-free geometry, and specifically that Jacobian alignment beats concept-correlation/probe accuracy. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between each candidate predictor and ground-truth steerability, with bootstrap CIs, per model and pooled, on the held-out test set. Convincing result: Jacobian alignment attains rho >= 0.5 AND exceeds the concept-correlation/probe-AUROC rho by >= 0.2, with concept-correlation's rho within [-0.2, 0.2] (replicating the "decodable but inert" anomaly). Decision band: Jacobian rho in [0.3, 0.5], or its margin over concept-correlation in [0.1, 0.2] -> suggestive; report as a weak predictor. Negative result (concept-correlation predicts as well as Jacobian alignment) refutes the specific claim; if NO predictor beats rho 0.3, steerability is closer to noise. Controls/baselines compared: effective read-out through downstream attention/MLP input weights, decoder-direction norm relative to typical residual norm, raw-gradient cosine, a value-vs-pointer logit-effect-geometry class, and a random-subspace control; we also report partial correlation controlling for feature strength/decodability so any gain is not a proxy for magnitude.

Experiment 2 (H2 - causal test via synthetic directions): Tests whether Jacobian alignment causes steerability rather than merely correlating. Decisive metric: steerability difference between matched-decodability directions constructed with high vs low Jacobian alignment (low-alignment made by orthogonalizing a decodable direction against the top Jacobian subspace). Convincing result: high-alignment synthetic directions steer (slope > 0 with CI excluding 0) while low-alignment ones are inert (slope indistinguishable from the random-direction control), a monotone effect of alignment across >= 4 alignment levels. Decision band: a monotone trend present but low-alignment directions still steer at >= half the high-alignment slope -> alignment contributes but is not the whole story. Negative result (steerability independent of imposed alignment) refutes the account. We vary intervention layer to check the predictor tracks the layer-dependence of steerability, re-measuring alignment post-construction to confirm the manipulation took.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a pre-flight filter saves screening compute): Tests that ranking directions by the best cheap predictor finds steerable directions without generation-based screening. Decisive metric: precision@10 for actually-steerable directions under the steerability-score ranking. Convincing result: precision@10 >= 0.8, at least 2x the concept-correlation ranking and above random, with generation runs avoided to find 10 good directions >= 50%. Decision band: precision@10 in [0.5, 0.8] -> a useful but imperfect screen. Negative result (precision@10 <= random) refutes H3. Reported per model on the held-out set.

Experiment 4 (H4 - cross-domain generality): Tests whether the predictor's utility holds across protein, antibody, and molecule families. Decisive metric: the Experiment-1 Spearman rho within each family. Convincing result: rho >= 0.4 in all three families. Decision band: rho >= 0.4 in two of three -> partial generality; narrow the headline claim to the families where it holds. Negative result (holds in only one family) means the principle is family-specific, a scientifically informative limit rather than a universal law.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Jacobian alignment requires a differentiable property signal; for properties only measurable by non-differentiable evaluators (HMMER motifs, folding) we substitute a lightweight differentiable surrogate predictor, which may introduce approximation error - we quantify surrogate fidelity and check robustness to surrogate choice. 2) The predictor may be property- or layer-specific rather than universal; we mitigate by testing multiple properties, three layers, and three model families and reporting where it fails, and by narrowing the claim to the supported setting. 3) In-silico steerability and validity are proxies for wet-lab outcomes; claims concern model-internal controllability, not experimental function. 4) The synthetic-direction ablation assumes orthogonalization cleanly removes Jacobian alignment without side effects; we verify by re-measuring alignment post-construction. 5) We present Jacobian alignment as an empirically validated, falsifiable predictor motivated by the intuition that only read directions can causally act - not as a derived theorem; if concept-correlation predicts equally well in some models, the anomaly may be architecture-dependent, which we would still report as informative.

Name: intervention_leak_scientific_design
Title: Does Clamping Fix It? Auditing Whether Interpretable-Feature Interventions Truly Eliminate Undesired Properties in Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: In safety-critical scientific design, an intervention believed to remove a hazardous property (a toxic substructure, an instability motif, a disallowed fold) frequently fails at the object level: when we clamp/ablate the interpretable feature that encodes it, the model reconstitutes the property through alternative internal routes during iterative/autoregressive decoding. We hypothesize this leakage is substantial, arises SPONTANEOUSLY during ordinary generation (not only under adversarial optimization), and is predicted by concept redundancy - the effective rank of the concept subspace (how many independent SAE directions carry the concept), which is distinct from raw feature count or SAE reconstruction error. A redundancy-aware fix that clamps the whole concept subspace should close the leak.
Related Work: The top-line phenomenon that SAE interventions can be circumvented is not ours: a concurrent text-LLM paper (Cui et al. 2026, 'SAE Interventions are Unreliable: Post-Intervention Recovery') shows clamping an 'unsafe' feature in language models can be optimized around. Our delta is the scientific-object setting and spontaneous leakage. Almost all interpretability-for-design work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE, molecular-transformer SAE circuits, GFlowNet interpretation, chemical-LM steering vector fields, molecular task arithmetic) demonstrates that clamping/steering a feature CHANGES a target property, reporting success at the level of a forward pass or a single generation; dynamic-guardrail and side-effect-prediction work filters or predicts at the output rather than auditing whether the internal suppression itself holds through decoding. No prior work asks whether feature interventions ROBUSTLY eliminate undesired properties in SCIENTIFIC generative models, where 'recovery' is an objectively measurable structural fact rather than fuzzy text behavior, and where multi-step structured decoding (autoregressive SMILES, iterative diffusion denoising) provides many natural re-routing opportunities. We are the first to (i) define and measure intervention leakage for scientific object design, (ii) test whether it arises spontaneously during ordinary generation, and (iii) tie leakage to a pre-specified concept-redundancy metric, yielding a practical audit plus a redundancy-aware multi-feature clamping fix. Adopters: molecular design, protein engineering, and safety/interpretability researchers.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design increasingly relies on a hopeful assumption: that clamping or ablating an interpretable feature reliably removes the property it encodes - a load-bearing assumption when the property is a safety hazard. We stress-test it for scientific generative models, where 'the property' is an objectively verifiable structural fact: a toxic substructure in a molecule, a destabilizing motif in a protein, or a disallowed fold. We define intervention leakage as the rate at which a suppressed, undesirable property reappears in the FINAL generated object despite an active feature-level intervention, and ask how often an intervention thought to remove a hazardous motif still yields a dangerous final candidate. Using autoregressive SMILES chemical LMs and ESM-2 protein LMs with sparse autoencoders, we clamp features a forward-pass analysis identifies as encoding a target undesired property, run ordinary iterative generation, and check finished objects with hard structural evaluators (RDKit substructure matching, HMMER/regex motifs, DSSP/ESMFold). We hypothesize leakage is substantial and arises during NORMAL decoding rather than only under adversarial optimization, because the model re-encodes the concept through alternative features at later positions/denoising steps. We further hypothesize leakage is predicted by concept redundancy - the effective rank of the concept subspace, pre-specified and shown to predict beyond property frequency, SAE sparsity, and classifier confidence - and validate a redundancy-aware fix that clamps the concept subspace rather than a single feature, on held-out properties and models. We report leakage rates, a redundancy-based reliability predictor, and the validity/diversity cost of subspace clamping. Results turn feature interventions from an assumed-safe knob into an auditable, quantifiable one for safe scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (both frozen): (a) a GPT-style autoregressive SMILES chemical LM (~10M, trained on a ChEMBL/ZINC subset, or a public checkpoint) with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream at a mid layer; (b) ESM-2 150M/650M (masked protein LM) with a residual-stream TopK SAE. SAEs trained on 20M activation-tokens (500k-sequence/molecule subset), Adam lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, 3 SAE seeds. Undesired properties (concrete, with HARD model-independent evaluators): molecules - specific PAINS/toxicophore substructures (e.g., nitro/aromatic-amine toxicophore), a reactive Michael-acceptor group, or exceeding a ring/heteroatom bound (RDKit SMARTS); proteins - a specific catalytic/binding motif such as the Ser-His-Asp triad (HMMER/regex) and a disallowed secondary-structure target such as a forbidden beta-sheet content (DSSP on ESMFold). For each property, the single best encoding feature and the ranked set of features above a concept-correlation floor (the candidate concept subspace) are recorded via concept-correlation and probe AUROC on held-out objects. REDUNDANCY METRIC (pre-specified before results): effective rank of the concept subspace = participation ratio of the singular values from SVD of the correlated-feature activation matrix on held-out objects; reported alongside, but claimed distinct from, raw feature count and SAE reconstruction error. "Clamp" = fixing the feature to a strong suppressive value at every decoding step. Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - feature suppression leaks in the finished object): Tests whether clamping the best feature still lets the property appear in finished objects at rates single-forward-pass evidence would deem impossible. Falsifiable primary endpoint (fixed decoding settings, intervention strength, and property class): the forward-pass-vs-end-object gap = (Leakage Rate) minus (the residual property rate implied by the clamp's single-step logit/probe suppression), where Leakage Rate = fraction of FINISHED objects still containing the property under the hard evaluator despite the active clamp. Convincing result: gap >= 20 percentage points for at least half the target properties. Decision band: gap in [10, 20] points -> leakage present but modest; partial support. Negative result (gap < 10 points) means interventions are reliable - a valuable positive result about intervention fidelity, refuting the leak hypothesis. Data/systems: N = 2,000 objects per property, generated under conditions that naturally exhibit the property (property-biased sampling/seed contexts). Controls/baselines: (i) no intervention (baseline occurrence), (ii) the single-forward-pass 'success' estimate, (iii) random-feature clamp of matched activation magnitude, (iv) matched-capacity clamp (same number of directions, random). Robustness sweeps: clamp magnitude up to validity collapse, decoding temperature, and generation length. A re-routing trace on leaked objects (which alternative features carry high concept-probe activation where the property re-emerges) plus one-by-one ablation of those features confirming leakage drops identifies the leak paths.

Experiment 2 (H2 - redundancy predicts leakage): Tests that leakage is predictable from how redundantly the concept is encoded. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between per-property Leakage Rate and the pre-specified effective-rank redundancy score. Convincing result: redundancy rho >= 0.5 (CI excludes 0) while single-feature concept-correlation shows rho within [-0.2, 0.2]. Decision band: redundancy rho in [0.3, 0.5] -> suggestive. Negative result (redundancy no more predictive than concept-correlation) refutes H2. Crucial ablation: partial correlation showing redundancy predicts leakage BEYOND property base-frequency, SAE sparsity (k), and concept-classifier confidence. Data: tens of target properties per domain (many toxicophores/motifs) to power the regression, bootstrap CIs.

Experiment 3 (H3 - redundancy-aware suppression closes the leak): Tests that clamping the full concept subspace, not one feature, removes the leak. Decisive metric: Leakage Rate as a function of subspace dimension k (projecting out the top-k correlated directions). Convincing result: Leakage Rate falls monotonically with k and drops below 5% at modest k (k <= 8) while validity/diversity cost stays acceptable (RDKit-validity / pseudo-perplexity / ESMFold pLDDT within 10% of baseline, bounded off-target property drift, and generation diversity retained). Decision band: leakage reaches [5%, 15%] only at large k, or the k needed incurs cost beyond 10% -> the fix works at a price; report the leakage-validity frontier. Negative result (subspace clamping does not reduce leakage below single-feature clamping) undercuts the redundancy account. Generalization: the fix is validated on HELD-OUT properties and on a masked/diffusion generation setting to test whether iterative denoising leaks differently than autoregressive decoding.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hard evaluators define the property crisply, but restricting to properties with unambiguous structural evaluators limits generality; fuzzy properties (e.g., 'developability') are out of scope. 2) Leakage could be an artifact of weak clamping; mitigated by sweeping clamp magnitude to validity collapse and reporting leakage across the range, plus random-feature and matched-capacity clamp controls. 3) SAE quality and layer choice may confound which features 'encode' the property; controlled with multiple SAE architectures/layers and probe-based verification. 4) In-silico validity and property calls (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal controllability and structural facts, not experimental function. 5) The redundancy predictor could be underpowered with few properties; mitigated by tens of properties per domain and partial-correlation controls for base-frequency, sparsity, and classifier confidence. 6) If leakage is negligible, that is still a valuable positive result establishing intervention reliability, and the redundancy analysis explains why.

Name: interpretable_feature_bayesopt
Title: Optimizing in Concept Space: Do Interpretable SAE Features Make Scientific Design Optimization More Sample-Efficient and Auditable?
Short Hypothesis: Primary contribution: SAE-feature-space Bayesian optimization (BO) with a causal test of monosemanticity. We claim that running query-efficient BO with uncertainty (a Gaussian-process surrogate, not manual or greedy latent steering) directly over the sparse, monosemantic feature space of a sparse autoencoder trained on a frozen scientific foundation model yields more sample-efficient design than BO over the model's raw embeddings or a VAE latent, tested in two concrete settings: protein fitness optimization (ProteinGym/FLIP oracles) and small-molecule property optimization (penalized-logP, QED, docking). We further hypothesize that the per-dimension monosemanticity of the search space—defined quantitatively and pre-registered, not merely its dimensionality—causally predicts optimization efficiency, and that interpretability additionally enables concept-prior warm-starting and faithful, human-readable design trajectories that let a protein engineer choosing the next wet-lab construct see why each step was taken.
Related Work: Latent-space Bayesian optimization (LSBO) is a mature line: Automatic Chemical Design (Gomez-Bombarelli 2018), Constrained BO in VAE latent space (Griffiths & Hernandez-Lobato 2019), LaMBO (Stanton 2022), CLaSMO (2024), and low-dimensional semi-supervised latent BO for antimicrobial peptides (2025). Separately, SAE-steering work (InterPLM 2024, ProtSAE 2025, 'SAEs for Low-N Protein Function Prediction and Design' 2025, Steering Protein LMs/ASPO 2025) shows SAE latents can steer generation and even design high-fitness variants via manual latent steering. The crucial gap: (i) no prior work uses the INTERPRETABLE SAE feature space of a FROZEN foundation model as the actual optimization search space for closed-loop, oracle-guided Bayesian optimization; existing LSBO uses black-box VAE/embedding spaces, and the low-N SAE paper uses manual/greedy steering, not query-efficient BO with uncertainty. (ii) No one has tested whether the MONOSEMANTICITY of the search space is causally responsible for optimization efficiency, versus mere dimensionality reduction. (iii) No one exploits interpretability to warm-start BO with concept-property priors or to emit human-readable design trajectories. Our proposal isolates the value of interpretability as a search-space property, distinguishing it from generic dimensionality reduction, and from all prior LSBO and SAE-steering work. We further separate the interpretable-space claim from generic BO machinery by comparing against trust-region (TuRBO) and active-subspace BO run in every candidate space, and we validate on at least one real measured fitness landscape (ProteinGym/FLIP) rather than proxy oracles alone, so the efficiency claim is not an artifact of a particular optimizer or a synthetic oracle.
Abstract: Scientific design—of proteins, molecules, and sequences—is a query-efficiency problem: each oracle evaluation (an assay, a docking run, a simulation) is expensive, so the geometry of the search space decides how many experiments a designer must run. Latent-space Bayesian optimization (LSBO) searches the black-box latent of a task-specific VAE, while interpretability work shows sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose frozen foundation-model activations into monosemantic, concept-aligned features. We unify these threads: does query-efficient Bayesian optimization directly in an interpretable SAE feature space improve sample efficiency and auditability over optimizing in raw embeddings or a VAE latent? A Gaussian-process surrogate proposes points in the SAE space of a frozen ESM-2 (protein fitness) or a SMILES chemical LM (molecular properties), decodes them to activations, and generates candidates scored by in-silico oracles including a real ProteinGym/FLIP fitness assay. We compare against embedding-space BO, VAE-latent LSBO, trust-region and active-subspace BO, and genetic algorithms under matched oracle budgets. Our central causal test asks whether per-dimension monosemanticity—pre-registered and measured at fixed dimension against random rotations and PCA—drives efficiency, not dimensionality alone. We exploit interpretability two further ways: concept-prior warm-starting and faithful, human-readable design trajectories reporting which named concepts each step turned up or down, checked by counterfactual edits. The concrete payoff is fewer wet-lab constructs per hit for a protein engineer, plus an auditable rationale. We expect interpretable-feature BO to match or beat baselines on regret-at-budget while uniquely yielding controllable, auditable design paths—turning interpretability from a descriptive luxury into an optimization asset.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Encoders (frozen): for proteins, ESM-2 150M/650M with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream at the intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer; for molecules, a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~10M) with a residual-stream SAE. Encoding: object -> foundation-model activations -> SAE feature vector (mean-pooled). Decoding: SAE feature vector -> reconstructed activations -> object (masked infilling / activation-conditioned decoding for proteins; activation steering during autoregressive decoding for SMILES). Encode-decode round-trip fidelity (property-preservation rate on a held-out set) is verified and reported before optimization. Oracles (cheap): proteins - ESMFold pLDDT (validity), DSSP secondary-structure targets, GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability/fitness head, and FLIP/ProteinGym fitness tasks where available; molecules - RDKit logP, QED, penalized-logP, docking against one fixed target, synthetic accessibility. Every reported optimization run uses >= 20 random seeds. MONOSEMANTICITY (pre-registered before optimization): per-space score = mean over active dimensions of (concept-correlation of the dimension with its best-matching labeled concept) x (activation sparsity, the fraction of inputs on which the dimension is inactive); higher means each axis carries one clean concept. Real-benchmark anchor: at least one protein setting uses a published ProteinGym/FLIP fitness assay as the oracle (not a synthetic proxy), so efficiency gains are demonstrated on a real measured landscape.

Experiment 1 (H1 - SAE-space BO is more sample-efficient): Tests whether Bayesian optimization over the SAE feature space finds better designs per oracle call than BO over raw embeddings or a VAE latent. Decisive metric: oracle-calls-to-threshold (calls to first reach a fixed target property value), median over >= 20 seeds and multiple target properties; secondary regret-at-budget. Convincing result: SAE-space BO needs >= 30% fewer oracle calls than the best competing space, with the paired 95% CI excluding a tie. Decision band: reduction in [10%, 30%] -> a real but modest efficiency gain. Negative result (< 10% or slower) refutes H1. Systems, identical GP+Expected-Improvement (qEI for batches) and identical oracle budget: (a) SAE feature space, (b) raw foundation-model embeddings PCA-reduced to the SAE's active dimension (isolating space identity from dimension), (c) a task-trained VAE latent (LaMBO-style), (d) a discrete genetic algorithm on the object; and, to show the space effect is not tied to one optimizer, each space is additionally run with trust-region BO (TuRBO), active-subspace BO, and a random-feature-map GP. Validity retention along the trajectory and novelty/diversity of optima also reported.

Experiment 2 (H3 - monosemanticity, not dimensionality, drives efficiency): Tests the central claim by holding dimensionality fixed and varying only per-axis meaning. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between a per-space monosemanticity score (mean per-feature concept-correlation / activation sparsity) and optimization efficiency (area over the regret curve), across matched-dimension spaces and target properties. Convincing result: rho >= 0.5 at fixed dimension. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.5] -> suggestive. Negative result (rho within [-0.2, 0.2]) means dimensionality, not monosemanticity, was doing the work, refuting H3. Matched-dimension spaces: (i) SAE features (high monosemanticity), (ii) a random rotation of the SAE basis (same geometry/dimension, meaning destroyed), (iii) PCA components (dense, mixed), (iv) a partially trained/entangled SAE. Confounder controls: results hold or covary decoder reconstruction quality, local landscape smoothness (fitted GP lengthscale), SAE sparsity level k, and active dimensionality across spaces, so monosemanticity is not a proxy for any of them.

Experiment 3 (H4 - concept-prior warm-starting cuts oracle calls, only in the interpretable space): Tests whether known feature-property associations can warm-start the search. Decisive metric: oracle-calls-to-threshold, warm-start vs cold-start, in the SAE space. Convincing result: >= 25% fewer calls warm vs cold, and the baseline spaces (which lack named axes) cannot be warm-started the same way. Decision band: reduction in [10%, 25%] -> modest speedup. Negative result (no warm-start benefit) refutes H4. Warm-start initializes the GP prior mean / restricts the initial design region using concept-correlation associations; reported with and without label filtering to expose sensitivity to noisy labels.

Experiment 4 (H2 - auditable, faithful design rationales): Tests whether the interpretable space yields human-readable rationales that are actually faithful. Decisive metric: trajectory-faithfulness score = fraction of reported concept-changes whose ablation reproduces the predicted property-change direction. Convincing result: faithfulness >= 0.7, a deliverable the raw-embedding/VAE/GA baselines cannot produce at all. Decision band: faithfulness in [0.5, 0.7] -> partially trustworthy rationales. Negative result (< 0.5) means the rationales are post-hoc and unreliable, refuting the auditability claim. Each accepted BO step emits the top named concepts increased/decreased (annotation- or LLM-labeled) and the resulting property change. Beyond ablation, faithfulness is cross-checked by a counterfactual test—constructing objects with the named concept explicitly edited and confirming the property moves as predicted—and a small decision-usefulness check asking whether an annotator, given the rationale, picks the better of two candidates above chance. The full protocol is repeated across both domains and two model sizes for robustness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico oracles are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern sample-efficiency and auditability of optimization, not experimental validation. 2) SAE encode/decode round-trip fidelity may be lossy, capping achievable optima; we quantify reconstruction quality and report its correlation with performance, and use the best available SAE architecture. 3) The interpretable space could win merely by favorable dimensionality; the matched-dimension monosemanticity experiment (Experiment 2) is specifically designed to rule this out. 4) GP surrogates scale poorly to very high feature dimensions; we mitigate with sparsity-aware feature selection (optimize only over active/relevant features) and additive/trust-region GPs, reporting sensitivity to this choice. 5) Concept-prior warm-starting depends on the quality of feature-property labels, which may be noisy; we report warm-start gains with and without label filtering. 6) If interpretable-feature BO merely ties baselines on regret, the auditability and warm-start results still constitute a meaningful, publishable contribution establishing interpretability as a 'free' optimization asset.

Name: cross_model_steering_transfer
Title: Steer Small, Design Big: Transferring Validated Interpretable Steering Directions Across Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: Two testable subclaims. (1) Alignment transfers directions: because SAE feature spaces are approximately universal across models (similar under rotation-invariant alignment), a linear/rotation map learned from paired activations carries a property-linked steering direction from a small, cheap generative model to a larger or different-architecture one. (2) Causal steerability survives transfer: the transferred direction not only points the right way but actually steers the target model's GENERATED objects to the same property, and a direction's steerability on the small model predicts its steerability on the large one—so cheap models act as steerability-screening proxies, letting protein- and molecule-design teams validate design controls once on inexpensive models and deploy them on state-of-the-art ones without re-running per-model screening.
Related Work: Two lines converge here. (1) SAE steering of scientific generative models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; Steering PLMs/ASPO 2025; ProtoMech cross-layer transcoders 2026; SAEs for low-N design 2025) all discover and validate steering directions SEPARATELY per model, requiring costly per-model SAE training and generation-based screening. (2) Feature-space universality work (Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across LLMs via SAEs, 2024) shows SAE feature subspaces are similar across text LLMs under rotation-invariant transforms and conjectures—but never demonstrates for generation—that steering vectors might transfer. No prior work (a) tests whether interpretable steering directions transfer BETWEEN scientific generative models to control the properties of GENERATED objects, (b) exploits a cheap model as a steerability-screening proxy for an expensive one, or (c) quantifies the design-efficiency savings of not re-discovering steerable features per model. The concurrent DiMaS (2026) finding that features are 'linearly decodable but not linearly steerable' makes the transfer-of-steerability question especially non-trivial and worth testing. Our proposal turns universality from a descriptive observation into a practical cross-model design tool. We keep the distinctions sharp: text-LM transfer studies alignment of representations or activation-steering effects but never the property-validity of generated scientific objects; SAE-universality work measures subspace similarity but not transferred causal steerability; and prior protein SAE steering validates directions per model. We therefore report calibration curves showing exactly when source steerability predicts target steerability, and treat transfer failures as first-class findings.
Abstract: Steering interpretable features to control generated proteins and molecules currently demands an expensive, model-specific pipeline: train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), screen thousands of features for the few that actually steer, and validate on the target model. As foundation models grow, this per-model screening cost dominates controllable design. We ask whether it can be paid once on a small model and amortized: given that SAE feature spaces are approximately universal across models, can a steering direction discovered and causally validated on a small, cheap model be aligned and transferred to steer a larger or different-architecture model? Our pipeline (1) discovers and causally validates directions on a small model (e.g., ESM-2 35M) with cheap in-silico oracles; (2) learns a rotation/linear alignment between the small and large models' activation spaces from a shared held-out corpus; (3) maps the validated direction into the large model and steers generation. We evaluate across protein-LM sizes (ESM-2 35M->150M->650M), across architectures (masked ESM-2 <-> autoregressive protein LM), and on a molecular SMILES pair, using pre-registered model pairs and properties. We measure transfer efficiency (fraction of native steering effect recovered), validity retention, and—crucially—whether small-model steerability predicts large-model steerability, enabling cheap screening. We report how many candidate directions can be filtered before expensive validation and the compute saved, and treat low-transfer regimes as informative limits of feature universality. Adopters are protein-design, molecular-generation, and mechanistic-interpretability groups who could screen design controls on inexpensive models and deploy them on state-of-the-art ones, cutting the compute cost of controllable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Protein models (frozen): ESM-2 at 35M, 150M, 650M (same family, three sizes) and an autoregressive protein LM (ProtGPT2 or p-IgGen) for cross-architecture transfer. Molecule models: two GPT-style SMILES LMs of different sizes/tokenizers. Oracles: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability proxy (light fine-tuned head), motifs (HMMER/regex, e.g. zinc-finger); molecules - RDKit logP, QED, ring count, functional-group presence. Validity: ESMFold pLDDT and pseudo-perplexity (proteins), RDKit-validity (molecules). Source-model discovery: TopK SAEs (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the small model's residual stream (intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer); per property, candidate directions (SAE features + difference-of-means) are causally validated by a strength sweep measuring property gain vs validity, recording each direction's native steerability. Alignment map T between source and target residual spaces is learned from paired per-position activations on a shared held-out corpus (Procrustes/ridge, plus a rotation-invariant variant), with alignment quality reported as SVCCA and held-out reconstruction R^2; sensitivity to paired-corpus size is swept. Ablations also sweep alignment method (Procrustes/ridge/rotation-invariant) and alignment layer. Pre-registration: the model pairs (three same-family size pairs, the cross-architecture pair, the molecular pair), the target properties, and the success thresholds/failure modes are fixed before any transfer is measured. Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a validated direction transfers to steer the larger/other model): Tests whether a direction discovered and causally validated on the cheap model, mapped through T, steers the target model to the same property without re-screening on the target. Decisive metric: Transfer Efficiency TE = (target property gain from the transferred direction) / (target property gain from a direction natively discovered and validated on the target). Convincing result: TE >= 0.7 for same-family size pairs and >= 0.5 for cross-architecture pairs, each exceeding all controls. Decision band: TE in [0.4, 0.7] (same-family) or [0.3, 0.5] (cross-architecture) -> partial transfer; report as usable-with-loss. Negative result (TE < 0.4 same-family, or < 0.3 cross-architecture, or not above controls) refutes H1 for that regime. Systems/controls: (a) random-direction transfer through T, (b) naive same-index feature transfer without alignment, (c) no steering, (d) the source direction inserted into the target WITHOUT the alignment map (unaligned control); tested across all size pairs, cross-architecture pairs, and the molecular pair. Absolute property gain, validity retention, and novelty/diversity also reported.

Experiment 2 (H2 - cheap models as steerability-screening proxies): Tests whether source-model steerability predicts target-model steerability, so the small model can pre-select which directions will steer the big one. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between source-model native steerability and target-model steerability of the transferred direction (and of the natively rediscovered counterpart). Convincing result: rho >= 0.5, with precision@10 >= 0.7 for using the small model to pick the target's steerable directions, and compute saved (big-model generation runs avoided to find 10 good directions) >= 50%. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.5] or precision@10 in [0.5, 0.7] -> a useful but noisy proxy. Negative result (rho <= 0.3 or precision@10 near random) refutes H2. Data: a large per-property direction bank (tens of directions) across the size and architecture pairs, bootstrap CIs.

Experiment 3 (H1 robustness - transfer preserves compositionality; and failure analysis): Tests whether jointly transferring 2-3 directions preserves multi-constraint control on the target, and characterizes where transfer breaks. Decisive metric: joint constraint-satisfaction rate on the target under transferred directions, versus the same on natively validated directions. Convincing result: transferred joint satisfaction >= 0.7x the native joint satisfaction with comparable interference. Decision band: [0.4, 0.7]x -> partial preservation. Negative result (< 0.4x) means transfer does not carry compositional control. Failure analysis reports which property types and layer/architecture pairs fail and whether alignment quality (SVCCA/R^2) predicts Transfer Efficiency - a scientifically informative characterization of the limits of feature universality even under a broadly negative outcome.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cross-architecture representation spaces (masked vs autoregressive; different tokenizers) may be too dissimilar for a linear alignment; we mitigate by also testing same-family size-scaling transfer (easier) and reporting where the linear assumption fails, which is itself informative. 2) In-silico oracles/validity are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal controllability and design compute-efficiency, not experimental viability. 3) Alignment may require a sizable paired-activation corpus; we quantify sensitivity to corpus size and use held-out objects to avoid leakage. 4) The DiMaS finding that features can be decodable-but-not-steerable means some directions may fail to transfer steerability even if the property signal transfers; we treat this as a measured outcome (the steerability-proxy test) rather than an assumption. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; we control with multiple layers and both SAE-feature and difference-of-means directions. 6) If transfer efficiency is low, the negative result still provides a valuable, publishable characterization of the limits of feature universality for controllable generation.

Name: causal_timing_window_design
Title: The Right Feature at the Right Time: Causal Intervention Windows for Interpretable Control of Biomolecular Diffusion Models
Short Hypothesis: Our claim is not the general idea that timing matters (already established for image/text diffusion) but a biomolecule-specific stratification law plus a hard-property causal test. During iterative diffusion generation of proteins and molecules, each interpretable feature has a distinct CAUSAL WINDOW—a range of denoising timesteps where clamping it actually decides an objectively verifiable property (fold topology, secondary-structure content, a motif, a functional group), outside of which the same intervention is inert or destroys validity. We hypothesize (i) a stratification law: property classes order by window—coarse/topological properties decided early, fine/local properties late—more sharply than in pixel-space diffusion because biomolecular validity is a hard physical constraint; and (ii) intervening only inside a feature's causal window hits the target property with far higher validity and far fewer wasted intervention steps than steering uniformly across all timesteps or at a single pass.
Related Work: Image-diffusion interpretability shows temporally-structured concept emergence: 'Emergence and Evolution of Interpretable Concepts in Diffusion Models' (2025) finds composition locks in early and style mid-process; TIDE (2025) builds temporal-aware SAEs; 'Unraveling the Temporal Dynamics of the Unet' (2023) finds composition/denoising phases. DLM-Scope (2026) does diffusion-time SAE steering for text but does not characterize property-specific causal windows. In the scientific-object space, all steering work (InterPLM 2024, ProtSAE 2025, ProtoMech 2026, antibody-SAE 2025, automated-neuron-labelling 2025) either uses masked/autoregressive models with single-pass interventions or applies steering uniformly, and none studies WHEN during a diffusion denoising trajectory an interpretable feature is causally decisive for a hard, verifiable property. The protein-DPO paper (2026) reports a training-time temporal decoupling of structure vs property, but concerns fine-tuning dynamics, not inference-time feature interventions. We are the first to (a) map property-class-specific causal intervention windows for interpretable features in biomolecular diffusion generation, (b) show that window-targeted intervention beats uniform/single-pass steering on the validity–control frontier, and (c) turn timing into an efficiency lever (fewer intervention steps, cheaper compute) for scientific design. The exact delta from the closest prior family (temporal-SAE and diffusion-time steering papers on images/text): they show concepts emerge at different times and can be steered per-timestep, but never establish, on a hard verifiable property, a per-feature window OUTSIDE of which intervention is causally inert, nor a property-class stratification law, nor an efficiency accounting of intervention steps saved.
Abstract: Controllable design of proteins and molecules increasingly clamps interpretable features to hit target properties, but nearly all methods apply the intervention at the same strength at every step of an iterative generative process—wasting compute and often breaking validity. Work on image diffusion shows interpretable concepts emerge and lock in at different stages (composition early, style late), implying that WHEN you intervene matters as much as WHAT. We ask whether biomolecular diffusion models have analogous property-specific causal windows and whether exploiting them makes design more valid and efficient. Using protein diffusion models and a SMILES/graph molecular diffusion model, we train sparse autoencoders on per-timestep denoiser activations, link features to hard, verifiable properties (secondary structure, fold topology, motifs; ring systems, functional groups, logP band), and measure each feature's causal effect on the finished object when clamped only within a sliding timestep window—yielding a Causal Timing Map. We test two hypotheses: (1) a stratification law, coarse/topological properties decided early and fine/local ones late; (2) window-targeted intervention Pareto-dominates uniform and single-pass steering on a control-validity frontier while using far fewer intervention steps. A designer who wants a specific fold AND a late-stage functional motif would otherwise fight interference by steering everything everywhere; a timing schedule assigns each property to its window instead. We report timing maps, frontier comparisons, an accounting of intervention steps saved, and a simple scheduling recipe—establishing timing as a first-class, efficiency-boosting control axis for interpretable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Generators (both instrumentable for per-step denoiser activations, frozen): (a) a discrete/masked protein diffusion or order-agnostic protein LM (a masked-diffusion ESM-style model or a DPLM-type model) and (b) a molecular diffusion model over SMILES/graphs. Hard automated evaluators so "the property in the finished object" is unambiguous: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), a fold-topology/contact-order proxy, GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex, e.g. zinc-finger); molecules - ring count / aromatic-ring presence, specific functional groups (RDKit SMARTS), a logP band, QED. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT and pseudo-perplexity (proteins); RDKit-validity and synthetic accessibility (molecules). Temporal SAEs: TopK SAEs (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the denoiser residual stream, both a timestep-shared variant and a temporally-conditioned (TIDE-style) variant, at the intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer; reconstruction fidelity and per-timestep concept-correlation with each hard property reported on held-out generations. "Clamp within a window" = fixing a feature to a strong value only for timesteps inside a specified window. Generation seeds: 5; 200 objects per condition.

Experiment 1 (H1 - each feature has a distinct causal window): Tests whether clamping a property-linked feature decides the finished-object property only inside a specific timestep window and is inert or destructive outside it. Decisive metric: window-localized causal effect = property change in the finished object per intervened step, as a function of window position/width (the Causal Timing Map). Convincing result: for >= 70% of property features there exists a window whose per-step effect is >= 2x the effect of clamping uniformly across the whole trajectory, AND clamping only outside that window changes the property by < 25% of the in-window effect. Decision band: an above-baseline window exists but its per-step effect is only 1.3-2x uniform -> weak localization; report as partial support. Negative result (no window beats uniform clamping) refutes H1. Data: non-overlapping timestep bins covering the trajectory plus growing/shrinking windows, per feature, with strength swept inside each window so timing effects are reported controlling for steering strength. Controls disentangle timing from confounds: a random/non-semantic-feature clamp (matched activation magnitude) must show no localized window, and window-localized effects are compared across properties of matched difficulty and features of matched prevalence, so a 'window' is not merely an easy-property or high-prevalence artifact.

Experiment 2 (H2a - properties stratify by window: coarse early, fine late): Tests whether coarse/topological properties are decided earlier than fine/local ones. Decisive metric: difference in mean causal-window center (as a fraction of the trajectory) between coarse properties (fold class, overall structure content, scaffold ring system) and fine ones (a single motif, one functional group), from a mixed-effects regression of window-center on property class. Convincing result: coarse centers earlier by >= 15% of the trajectory with the 95% CI excluding 0, in both domains. Decision band: difference in [5%, 15%] of the trajectory -> a trend, not decisive. Negative or reversed result (fine decided as early or earlier) refutes H2a but is still an informative characterization. We also test whether window center aligns with when the feature's concept-correlation first becomes predictive of the final object during unsteered generation.

Experiment 3 (H2b - window-targeted intervention dominates uniform/single-pass and saves steps): Tests whether intervening only inside each feature's mapped window beats standard uniform or single-pass steering. Decisive metric: control-validity frontier area (property success rate vs validity retention). Convincing result: window-targeted steering dominates the frontier AND uses >= 40% fewer intervention steps than uniform steering at matched property success. Decision band: frontier parity but >= 40% fewer steps, OR frontier dominance with < 40% step savings -> a partial win on one axis; report both. Negative result (no frontier or efficiency advantage) refutes H2b. Systems: (a) uniform steering across all timesteps, (b) single-pass/late-only steering, (c) window-targeted steering. Multi-property scheduling: for 2-3 properties with different windows, assign each to its own window and test whether temporal separation lowers interference versus co-applying all interventions at every step. Robustness across both domains, two checkpoints/sizes, and shared vs temporally-conditioned SAEs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Requires generators with accessible per-step activations; if a target model's diffusion process is not easily instrumented we substitute alternatives, limiting generality to instrumentable models. 2) In-silico evaluators (ESMFold, DSSP, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal causal timing and controllability, not experimental viability. 3) Causal windows may be entangled with steering strength; we sweep strength within each window and report timing effects controlling for strength. 4) Temporally-shared SAEs may blur timestep-specific features; we mitigate with temporally-conditioned SAEs and report differences. 5) The stratification hypothesis could fail (some fine properties decided early); a null or reversed result is still an informative, publishable characterization. 6) Feature-property linkage relies on concept-correlation, which can be non-causal; the sliding-window clamp is itself the causal test, so we treat correlation only as a candidate-selection step. 7) Efficiency gains depend on how much of the trajectory the causal window occupies; if windows are broad, savings shrink—this is directly quantified rather than assumed.

Name: internal_validity_foresight
Title: Failure Foresight: Do Interpretable Features Predict Invalid Scientific Generations Early Enough to Abort and Save Compute?
Short Hypothesis: The contribution is a compute-efficiency policy for VALIDITY, not merely the observation that features predict failure. During iterative/autoregressive generation of proteins and molecules, a small set of interpretable sparse-autoencoder features acts as an early internal 'validity alarm' predicting, well before generation completes, whether the finished object will be structurally INVALID—unfoldable, chemically invalid, degenerate. Unlike toxicity or factual hallucination, structural invalidity is an unambiguous physical/chemical fact with a hard evaluator, which makes both the label and the abort decision crisp. Monitoring these features enables a cheap early-abort-and-restart policy that raises valid objects produced per unit compute far above running every generation to completion, and does so more efficiently and interpretably than output-probability or perplexity-based early stopping or a compute-matched black-box probe.
Related Work: A large body of interpretability work uses SAE features to detect and mitigate hallucinations in text and vision-language models (RAGLens 2025; SSL/SAVE/SAFE 2025; 'Do I Know This Entity?' 2024; H-Neurons 2025) and to detect hallucinations early from internal states in factual QA (Varshney et al. 2024; MHAD 2024; HaMI 2025; HD-NDEs 2025). Separately, interpretability-for-design work on proteins/molecules (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; ProtoMech 2026; molecular-LM SAEs) focuses on STEERING features to add properties, and evaluates validity only as a side constraint. No prior work (a) treats interpretable features as a predictive EARLY-WARNING signal for the objective, structurally-verifiable INVALIDITY of a to-be-generated scientific object, (b) uses that signal to drive an early-abort-and-restart policy that improves valid-yield-per-compute, or (c) compares such interpretable monitoring against output-probability/perplexity early-stopping baselines on a compute-efficiency frontier.
