We convert the 'model self-knowledge' insight from the text-hallucination literature into a concrete, compute-saving reliability tool for scientific design, where validity is an unambiguous physical/chemical fact rather than fuzzy factuality. No prior SAE-auditing or early-failure-detection paper frames the decision as a compute-allocation policy—an abort-and-restart frontier trading detector cost and false-abort rate against generation budget saved—so that contribution is not covered by existing hallucination-detection or interpretability-auditing work.
Abstract: Generative models for scientific design routinely emit invalid objects—proteins that do not fold, molecules that violate chemistry, degenerate sequences—and practitioners pay the full cost of generation and validation before discovering the failure, wasting large fractions of a screening budget. We ask whether a model's own interpretable internal features reveal, early in generation, that it is heading toward an invalid object, and whether acting on that signal saves substantial compute. Building on evidence that sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features encode a form of model self-knowledge, we train SAEs on intermediate activations of protein and molecular generators and search for a compact 'validity-alarm' feature set whose early activations predict the eventual validity of the finished object, verified by hard structural evaluators (ESMFold pLDDT and pseudo-perplexity; RDKit validity and synthetic accessibility). We evaluate two claims separately: (i) alarm features forecast invalidity earlier and more accurately than output-probability/perplexity signals and at least as well as a compute-matched black-box probe; and (ii) an early-abort-and-restart controller built on them Pareto-dominates run-to-completion and output-side early stopping on the valid-objects-per-compute frontier, after charging the detector's own overhead. Probability-based stopping reacts only to output-side uncertainty and a black-box probe is opaque; interpretable alarms are both earlier and human-readable, yielding failure diagnoses (e.g., frustrated partial structures). First adopters are protein- and molecule-generation teams running large in-silico screens who need higher valid throughput per GPU-hour. Results would establish interpretable features as a practical reliability-and-efficiency layer for scientific generation.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Generators (instrumentable for per-step activations, frozen): (a) a protein generator - an autoregressive protein LM (ProtGPT2/p-IgGen) and/or a masked-diffusion protein LM; (b) a molecular generator - a GPT-style SMILES LM and/or a SMILES/graph diffusion model. Hard automatic VALIDITY labels for finished objects: proteins - ESMFold pLDDT above threshold AND pseudo-perplexity below threshold AND non-degenerate (low repeat/entropy); molecules - RDKit parseable/valence-valid AND passing basic sanity (SA score, ring/atom-count bounds). Corpus: 20k generations per model under normal sampling, saving full per-step activation trajectories, giving a balanced valid/invalid set. TopK SAEs (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream at a mid layer (intrinsic-dimension-elbow). At each progress fraction (10/25/50/75%) each SAE feature's mutual information / AUROC about eventual validity is measured on a training split, and a compact "validity-alarm" feature set is selected by information; all thresholds are fixed on a held-out split. Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - SAE features are an early validity alarm): Tests whether a small SAE-feature set forecasts eventual invalidity well before generation completes, earlier than output-side signals and competitively with a black-box probe. Decisive metric: forecast AUROC of the alarm features as a function of generation-progress fraction, summarized as the earliest progress fraction reaching AUROC 0.8. Convincing result: alarm features reach AUROC 0.8 at <= 50% progress, earlier (by >= 10% of the trajectory) than the best output-side signal and within 0.03 AUROC of a black-box MLP probe on raw activations, while remaining sparse. Decision band: AUROC-0.8 point in (50%, 75%] progress, or an earliness margin in [3%, 10%] of the trajectory -> foresight exists but is late/marginal. Negative result (never reaches AUROC 0.8 before completion, or no earlier than output-side signals) refutes H1. Baselines at the same progress point: running token log-probability, partial pseudo-perplexity, predictive entropy, and the raw-activation MLP probe (matched for parameter count and inference compute). Results are stratified by failure type (gross degenerate vs subtle near-miss invalidity) to report where foresight is easy versus hard. Alarm-feature interpretability is checked by auto-labeling top features and confirming faithfulness (clamping the feature shifts validity outcomes).

Experiment 2 (H2+H3 - early-abort-and-restart raises valid yield per compute, beating perplexity-based stopping): Tests whether monitoring the alarm features to abort-and-restart produces more valid objects per unit compute than running to completion and than output-side early stopping. Decisive metric: number of VALID objects produced per unit compute (total forward/decoding steps and ESMFold calls avoided, NET of the SAE monitoring overhead—the extra encoder passes—so 'compute saved' already charges the detector's cost), traced as a frontier over the abort threshold. Convincing result: the SAE-alarm controller yields >= 20% more valid objects per unit compute than run-to-completion and strictly beats output-probability/perplexity early stopping, while retaining >= 90% of the run-to-completion set's diversity/novelty and reporting the false-abort rate (valid generations wrongly killed). Decision band: improvement in [5%, 20%] over run-to-completion, or a tie with perplexity stopping -> a modest or contested gain. Negative result (no compute-frontier improvement, or diversity collapses below 90%) refutes H2/H3. Systems on the same frontier: (a) run-to-completion, (b) output-probability/perplexity-threshold stopping, (c) black-box raw-activation-probe abort, (d) random-abort at matched abort rate. Conditional/steered setting: repeat the frontier comparison when generation is steered toward a target property (invalidity more frequent), testing whether the alarm features remain useful precisely when validity is scarce.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Validity labels from ESMFold/RDKit are in-silico proxies for wet-lab viability; claims concern model-defined structural validity and generation efficiency, not experimental function. 2) Early prediction may be easy for gross degenerate failures but hard for subtle ones; we stratify results by failure type and report where foresight is impossible. 3) SAE-feature alarms might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; even so, sparsity, interpretability, and compute-frontier gains constitute the contribution—and we report this honestly. 4) Restart-based abort assumes generations are roughly i.i.d. in cost; for conditional generation restarts may correlate—mitigated by seed/prompt diversification and reported. 5) Aborting could bias the output distribution (collapse diversity); we explicitly measure diversity/novelty retention. 6) Requires generators with accessible intermediate activations, limiting scope to instrumentable open models. 7) Threshold tuning could overfit; we select thresholds on a held-out split and report frontier robustness across seeds.

Name: causal_correlational_discrepancy
Title: When the Model Disagrees with the Textbook: Using Interpretable-Feature Interventions to Discover Causal Structure-Property Rules That Contradict Correlational Biophysics
Short Hypothesis: Framed as discrepancy-as-discovery: sparse-autoencoder features of scientific foundation models encode two kinds of structure-property associations—those that merely reflect training-data correlations and those the model uses causally during generation—and the DISAGREEMENTS between them are a hypothesis-generation engine for design rules, not just an auditing signal. By contrasting a feature's CORRELATIONAL association with a property (co-occurrence) against its CAUSAL effect (property change of the generated object when the feature is clamped), we systematically surface DISCREPANT features: an established correlational structure-property rule the model does not causally exploit (candidate spurious), or a causal rule with no catalogued correlational basis (candidate novel). We hypothesize such discrepancies are numerous, are enriched for genuinely confounded/non-causal rules when validated against independent physics-based counterfactuals, and yield candidate causal design rules that outperform correlational-only rules as steering levers.
Related Work: Two lines are relevant. (1) SAE feature discovery in scientific models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology' 2025; the chemistry-LM SAE 2025; motif-gated domain-recognition causal patching 2025) shows features correlate with biological/chemical concepts and that some are causally necessary for a PREDICTION task. (2) Latent causal discovery (PerturbLearn attribute graphs 2022; active causal ML for molecules 2024) extracts causal graphs among attributes. Crucially, all discovery work either (a) reports concept-CORRELATION of features, or (b) verifies causal effect for a single prediction task, but NO work systematically contrasts a feature's correlational property-association with its causal generative effect to identify DISCREPANCIES, nor uses those discrepancies as a filter for finding structure-property rules that are correlational-but-not-causal (spurious) versus causal-but-uncatalogued (novel). Prior steering work treats agreement between correlation and causation as assumed; we treat their DISAGREEMENT as the scientific signal. This reframes interpretability from cataloguing what the model represents to auditing which structure-property rules are actually causal, and validates the model's verdicts against independent physics-based counterfactuals - a genuinely new use of feature interventions. The exact gap: prior auditing/causal-feature work diagnoses that some features are inert or causally necessary for a PREDICTION, but none MINES the systematic disagreement between correlation and causation to GENERATE new, testable structure-property hypotheses and then adjudicate them with an oracle independent of the model.
Abstract: Structure-property rules are the backbone of protein and molecular design, yet many textbook rules are correlational and may not reflect causal mechanism—so designers waste effort on heuristics that do not transfer. Scientific foundation models have absorbed enormous data and, through sparse autoencoders (SAEs), expose interpretable features linked to structural and property concepts. We use these features to audit and DISCOVER structure-property rules by contrasting two quantities per feature: its CORRELATIONAL association with a property (co-occurrence across natural objects) and its CAUSAL effect on the property of GENERATED objects when the feature is clamped. Features where these disagree—strong correlation but weak causal effect, or strong causal effect with weak correlation—are 'discrepant' and, we hypothesize, are enriched for spurious (confounded) or previously-uncatalogued causal design rules. We instantiate this on ESM-2 protein LMs and a SMILES chemistry LM with residual-stream SAEs and cheap in-silico evaluators. For each discrepant feature we emit a design-rule hypothesis and adjudicate it with a physics-based counterfactual test—matched object pairs differing only in the feature-linked structural element, scored by an oracle NOT derived from the model—to decide whether the model's causal verdict or the correlational rule is right. We report the rate and structure of discrepancies, their enrichment for known confounded rules (positive controls), whether causal-but-low-correlation features steer new designs where correlational rules fail, and case studies of candidate novel rules. Adopters—computational biophysicists and protein/chemical design teams—gain faster rule discovery, fewer spurious heuristics, and better candidate prioritization; the framework turns feature interventions into an auditable engine for discovering and stress-testing design rules.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (frozen): ESM-2 150M/650M with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream (intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer) and a GPT-style SMILES chemistry LM (~10M) with a residual-stream SAE; a Matryoshka SAE variant for robustness. SAEs trained on 20M activation-tokens from 500k-object subsets, 3 SAE seeds. Feature bank: interpretable, property-linked features selected by concept-correlation/probe AUROC on held-out natural objects. Cheap evaluators on FINISHED objects: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability proxy (light fine-tuned head), motif presence (HMMER/regex); molecules - RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, specific functional groups (SMARTS). For each (feature, property) pair: a Correlational score (point-biserial / mutual information between feature activation and property over a large natural sample) and a Causal score (property change per unit steer at low strength within the validity budget, from a strength sweep with unsteered and norm-matched random-direction controls; validity gated by pseudo-perplexity/pLDDT or RDKit-validity). Stability controls: discrepancy calls are tested for robustness to SAE feature split/merge instability by re-deriving both scores across 3 SAE seeds and the Matryoshka variant and reporting only discrepancies stable across seeds; a probe-based association is reported alongside concept-correlation as an alternative correlational measure, and random-direction features supply a null discrepancy rate. Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - discrepant features are numerous): Tests whether plotting correlational vs causal score surfaces many features where the two disagree. Decisive metric: discrepancy rate = fraction of (feature, property) pairs whose residual from the correlation=causation diagonal exceeds a noise band set by test-retest variance of the two scores. Convincing result: discrepancy rate >= 15% of pairs, with the off-diagonal mass beyond the noise band. Decision band: discrepancy rate in [5%, 15%] -> discrepancies exist but are uncommon. Negative result (< 5%, i.e. correlation tracks causation) is itself valuable, establishing that interpretable features faithfully track causal design rules, and refutes H1. Quadrants reported: (A) high-corr/low-causal (candidate spurious), (B) low-corr/high-causal (candidate uncatalogued causal), (C) concordant; rates broken out per domain, model size, SAE variant.

Experiment 2 (H2 - discrepancies are enriched for genuinely non-causal rules): Tests whether the discrepancy map recovers KNOWN spurious rules and whether an independent physics oracle sides with the model over the textbook on adjudicated cases. Decisive metric: agreement rate between the model's causal verdict and an independent physics adjudication on a sample of discrepant pairs. Convincing result: the discrepancy filter attains precision >= 0.7 on a labeled set (known-spurious rules landing in quadrant A, known-causal in C), AND physics adjudication agrees with the model's causal verdict on >= 70% of adjudicated discrepancies. Decision band: precision or agreement in [0.5, 0.7] -> partial validation. Negative result (near-chance precision/agreement) refutes H2. Data: a literature-curated set of known confounded and known causal structure-property associations (as many as the literature supports across both domains); matched counterfactual object pairs differing only in the feature-linked structural element (single-motif insert/delete or point substitutions for proteins; minimal SMARTS edits with matched scaffolds for molecules); the adjudication oracle (FoldX/Rosetta or MD-lite for proteins; RDKit/empirical logP or docking for molecules) is deliberately independent of the generative model's training signal; matching quality reported.

Experiment 3 (H3 - discrepancies are a design-rule engine): Tests whether quadrant-B causal-but-low-correlation features act as design levers where correlational-only rules fail. Decisive metric: success rate of producing the target property in NEW designs when steering the causal (quadrant-B) feature versus applying the correlational-only rule. Convincing result: causal-rule success >= 2x correlational-only success and >= 0.10 absolute. Decision band: causal-rule success between 1.2x and 2x correlational-only -> a real but modest advantage. Negative result (causal rules no better than correlational) refutes H3. Auto-generated human-readable candidate rules (feature label + measured causal effect) are the deliverable; robustness reported across two model sizes, two SAE architectures, and both domains.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico correlational and causal scores and physics adjudicators are all imperfect proxies; the strongest claim is triangulated agreement/disagreement among independent in-silico signals, not wet-lab truth. To reduce circularity, the adjudication oracle is deliberately chosen to be independent of the generative model's training signal. 2) Discrepancies could arise from SAE artifacts (entangled features, poor reconstruction) rather than genuine causal/correlational structure; we mitigate with multiple SAE architectures, probe verification, and random-direction controls. 3) Constructing clean matched counterfactuals is hard, especially for proteins where a single edit can change many things; we restrict to minimal, well-controlled edits and report matching quality. 4) The positive-control set of known spurious/causal rules may be small, limiting enrichment power; we include as many labeled rules as the literature supports across both domains. 5) A feature's causal score depends on layer/strength; we sweep strength within the validity budget and test layer sensitivity. 6) If discrepancies turn out to be rare (correlation almost always matches causation), that is itself a valuable, publishable result establishing that interpretable features faithfully track causal design rules.

Name: shared_concept_causal_bridge
Title: One Knob, Two Worlds: Do Proteins and Molecules Share Causally-Steerable Physicochemical Concepts in a Unified Sparse Autoencoder?
Short Hypothesis: Novelty boundary against shared-dictionary SAEs (USAE/SPARC/JSAE): the claim is not merely that a protein language model and a small-molecule language model share latent features, but that a SMALL set of well-grounded physicochemical concepts (hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity) is carried by SHARED interpretable directions that are CAUSALLY USABLE for bidirectional generation control—clamping one shared feature simultaneously and monotonically shifts the corresponding property in BOTH modalities' generations. We further hypothesize shared features are more causally steerable and validity-preserving than modality-private features encoding the same concept. We treat cross-modal feature HETEROGENEITY (a split dictionary) as a live contingency the study may find rather than an established sharing hypothesis: a low sharing rate is a reported, informative outcome, not a failure.
Related Work: Two threads meet here but have never been combined for causal generative control across scientific object types. (1) Cross-model/cross-modal SAEs—USAE (2025), SPARC (2025), and group-sparse multimodal SAEs (2026)—learn shared concept dictionaries across vision/language models, and 'Beyond Converging Representations' (2025) shows scientific foundation models across string/graph/3D/protein modalities are representationally aligned and collapse when extrapolating. (2) Single-modality scientific SAE steering—InterPLM (2024), the chemistry-LM SAE (2025), Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B (2025), CB-pLM (2024)—discovers and steers interpretable features WITHIN one model of one object type. Crucially: (a) all cross-modal SAE work is descriptive/retrieval-focused and never tests CAUSAL steering of generation; (b) all scientific steering work is confined to a single object type and never asks whether a concept has a single unified causal handle across proteins AND molecules. MolBind (2024) and protein-GDM alignment (2024) align modalities via contrastive learning but do not extract interpretable, individually-steerable, causally-validated shared features. We are the first to (i) train a unified SAE bridging a protein LM and a molecule LM, (ii) identify shared physicochemical concept features, and (iii) test whether ONE shared feature causally steers the SAME property in both modalities' generations—turning cross-modal interpretability from a similarity metric into a shared design lever. That closest negative finding—cross-modal representations align but collapse under extrapolation, and multimodal SAEs often learn split dictionaries—sets our null. We argue proteins and molecules may nonetheless share more transferable directions than vision-language pairs because both are governed by the SAME underlying physicochemical axes (hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity), a shared physical basis absent between pixels and text; whether that yields shared CAUSAL handles is exactly what we test.
Abstract: Physicochemical concepts—hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity—govern both proteins and small molecules, yet generative models for each are studied in isolation and steered by modality-specific machinery. We ask whether a single interpretable 'knob' controls the same property across worlds. Building on cross-model sparse autoencoders (USAE, SPARC), we train a unified SAE that jointly reconstructs the residual-stream activations of a protein language model (ESM-2) and a SMILES molecule language model, encouraging shared latents via cross-reconstruction and global sparsity. We identify SHARED features—dimensions active on a common concept in both modalities—versus modality-private ones. Our central test is causal: clamp a single shared feature and measure whether it simultaneously and monotonically shifts the property in BOTH protein generations (GRAVY, net charge, aromatic content) and molecule generations (logP, formal charge, aromatic-ring count), while preserving validity. A pre-registered success criterion defines 'shared' by thresholded concept agreement in both modalities, a minimum causal effect size, and correct cross-modal monotonicity on predefined property probes; we compare against independent SAEs, random shared features, matched private features, and per-modality difference-of-means, and ablate whether cross-reconstruction is necessary versus a simpler group-sparsity objective. If it holds, the payoff is a shared latent interface for cross-modal property control—transferring a validated concept-knob between lead optimization and protein redesign, and enabling cross-modal model debugging—plus mechanistic evidence for a modality-invariant physical abstraction in scientific foundation models. If sharing is low, we report which concepts resist unification, a clear and informative bound on cross-object conceptual structure.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Protein side (frozen): ESM-2 150M/650M; molecule side (frozen): a GPT-style SMILES chemistry LM (~10M, ChEMBL-trained). Residual-stream activations at a mid layer (intrinsic-dimension-elbow) collected for a large protein corpus (500k-sequence UniRef sample) and molecule corpus (500k-molecule ChEMBL/ZINC sample); no paired protein-molecule data is used - alignment is concept-level via the shared objective. Unified SAE: a joint TopK / global-TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) ingesting either modality with modality-specific encoder/decoder heads and a cross-reconstruction term (USAE/SPARC-style); a group-sparse variant for robustness; 3 SAE seeds. Baseline: two independent per-modality SAEs. Per-modality reconstruction fidelity and the fraction of cross-modally active latents (dictionary sharing rate) reported. Concept set {hydrophobicity, net charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity} with per-modality evaluators: proteins - GRAVY, net charge at pH7, aromatic-residue fraction, molecular weight, a polarity index (Biopython); molecules - RDKit logP, formal/partial charge, aromatic-ring count, MW, TPSA. Generation: masked infilling / activation-conditioned decoding (proteins), activation-steered autoregressive decoding (SMILES); 5 seeds. Pre-registration: the 5 concepts, their property evaluators, validity gates, layer choices, and statistical tests are fixed before causal measurement, and 'shared' requires passing the pre-declared concept-agreement, effect-size, and cross-modal monotonicity thresholds. An explicit ablation compares the cross-reconstruction objective against a plain shared/group-sparsity objective to test whether cross-reconstruction is necessary for shared causal handles.

Experiment 1 (H1 - shared concept directions exist in the joint SAE): Tests whether physicochemical concepts are carried by single latents active and property-correlated in BOTH modalities. Decisive metric: number of the 5 concepts admitting a SHARED feature (high concept-correlation in both modalities), and the sharing rate versus the independent-SAE baseline (which cannot produce shared indices). Convincing result: >= 3 of 5 concepts admit a shared feature, at a sharing rate above a co-labeling chance control. Decision band: 2 of 5 concepts shared -> partial sharing; report which concepts resist sharing. Negative result (<= 1 of 5, i.e. a split dictionary) refutes H1 but informatively bounds cross-modal abstraction. Matched modality-PRIVATE features (equally high correlation in only one modality) are recorded for Experiment 3.

Experiment 2 (H2 - one knob controls the property in both worlds): Tests whether clamping a single shared feature causally moves the property in each modality's generations. Decisive metric: bidirectional causal success rate = fraction of shared features that produce a significant, correctly-signed property shift in BOTH modalities. Convincing result: bidirectional causal success >= 0.5, exceeding random-direction and unrelated-feature controls, with consistent sign/monotonicity across modalities and validity retained (ESMFold pLDDT, pseudo-perplexity; RDKit-validity, SA). Decision band: bidirectional success in [0.3, 0.5] -> some shared knobs work; report which concepts. Negative result (< 0.3 or not above controls) means co-labeling did not imply a unified causal handle, refuting H2. Data: each shared feature clamped over a swept range, 200 objects per modality per setting.

Experiment 3 (H3 - shared features beat modality-private ones): Tests whether shared features are more steerable and validity-preserving than private features encoding the same concept. Decisive metric: control-validity Pareto frontier area for (i) the shared feature, (ii) the best matched modality-private feature, (iii) per-modality difference-of-means directions, per concept. Convincing result: the shared feature's frontier area is >= the best private feature's at equal validity for a majority of concepts, with better cross-modal steering-sign consistency. Decision band: shared within +-10% of private frontier area -> parity, not superiority; report as "shared no worse." Negative result (shared clearly below private) refutes H3. Supporting analyses: cross-modal steerability Spearman rho (does a shared feature's steerability in one modality predict the other; genuine handle if rho >= 0.5) and a transfer demo (validate a concept knob once on the cheap molecule model, apply the same shared feature to steer protein generation, report fraction of native effect recovered). Robustness across two protein sizes, two SAE variants, and layer choices.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico property evaluators and validity metrics (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal, cross-modal controllability, not experimental viability. 2) The joint SAE may learn a 'split dictionary' where most features stay modality-private (the known failure mode from multimodal SAE work); we mitigate with global-TopK and group-sparse objectives and report sharing rate honestly—a low sharing rate is itself an informative result about the limits of cross-modal abstraction. 3) A feature co-labeled as shared could reflect coincidental concept-correlation rather than a unified causal handle; the bidirectional causal test and cross-modal steerability-prediction analysis are designed to distinguish these. 4) Proteins and molecules have very different tokenizations and activation statistics, which may make joint reconstruction hard; we control by comparing to independent per-modality SAEs and reporting per-modality reconstruction fidelity. 5) Steering the molecule LM and masked/infilling protein generation are different decoding regimes; we standardize property measurement on finished objects and use random-direction controls to ensure comparability. 6) Layer/strength choices could confound sharing and steerability; we sweep strength within the validity budget and test multiple layers and SAE variants.
